title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
description: After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
description: Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is. — Jiachen Jiang, Coder
description: A coding agent deletes production data despite a written code freeze. Jiachen Jiang uses that incident to distinguish a request in a chat from an enforced boundary in the environment. An agent that still possesses destructive credentials can act on them, and logs it can edit are an unreliable account of what happened. Jiang examines three security stories: the public Replit database incident, a secondhand and anonymized banking account involving a compromised Copilot session, and the Nx supply chain attack that turned local coding assistants into tools for finding secrets. title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
description: A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, SonarSource
description: A coding agent can produce changes faster than the queues that test, review and merge them. Gautam Korlam examines that mismatch through his work on Uber's SubmitQueue and Gitar, now part of Sonar. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing combinations of changes before they land, but a process designed for human arrival rates can become a bottleneck when agents create many pull requests at once. title: Three Questions Every Agent Engineer Should Be Able To Answer
description: Jake Broekhuizen of LangChain Labs argues that owning your own intelligence comes down to three questions every agent engineer should be able to answer: where is your agent failing, how can you reliably make it fail again, and what needs to happen so it stops failing. title: Welcome to LangChain Academy
description:
Dive into self-paced, comprehensive courses designed to help you gain the relevant skills and knowledge to build, test, deploy, and monitor agents—no matter where you are in your agent development journey.

Get started for free → https://academy.langchain.com/

title: Building Engine v2: How LangChain approaches agent improvement
description: Ben Tannyhill, Product Manager at LangChain, explains how his team builds and evaluates LangSmith Engine, the agent in LangSmith that finds issues in production traces, proposes fixes, and creates evals to catch regressions. He covers the per-task benchmarks behind Engine's 2x better error identification on IssueBench, how the team runs Engine on LangChain's own go-to-market and coding agents and on Engine itself, and why a smaller model is sometimes the better choice for a simple task. title: Work with your team in ChatGPT Space
description: Explore a shared place to work with people and ChatGPT. See how Space brings conversations, context and collaborative work together.

title: Code review is no longer the bottleneck
description:
Code review is the new bottleneck. Codex brings pull requests, review feedback, and private conversations about your code into one place.

See how to find reviews across repositories, understand changes and risks, apply your team’s review guidelines, and draft comments without switching tools.

GitHub code review is generally available, with GitLab support in preview.

title: Set up your dot in the ChatGPT mobile app
description:
You can now create a dot from the ChatGPT mobile app. Set up your dot, edit the name, customize the avatar, and set your dot to be the first conversation you see when you open the ChatGPT app. 

Learn more about dots here: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots

title: From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
description:
From a four-billion-measurement Kaggle competition to models that recognize a molecule’s chemist, Leash Bio is testing what AI actually learns about chemistry. Co-founder and CEO Ian Quigley joins Brandon Anderson and RJ Honicky to explain how Leash makes DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) produce clean, reproducible protein–small-molecule binding data—and why collecting the right experiments matters as much as choosing a model.

title: Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
description:
From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.
